strengths: Combines two sensible ideas: a causal MLP-Mixer variant for time-series reconstruction and cluster-aware multi-embedding via spectral clustering of channel correlation profiles.
Evaluates on six standard anomaly-detection benchmarks and compares against many baselines, including recent transformer and MLP-Mixer-related methods.
Provides ablation studies on clustering, causal mixer, embedding mixer, and clustering variants, plus robustness runs over three seeds and GFLOPs.
Includes an honest limitations section discussing sensitivity to alpha, small-data issues, and incomplete spurious-correlation mitigation.
The anomaly-evidence accumulation is a practical adaptation of sequential detection ideas and shows modest improvements over point-based thresholding in Table 3.
weaknesses: The central 'online' claim is not supported: Appendix D states that the statistical-significance parameter alpha and threshold h are searched to maximize the best F1 score on the test data. This is test-set leakage and contradicts the paper's framing of an online, real-time detector. A genuinely online method would need threshold/alpha selection from validation or training data only.

There are unexplained result inconsistencies: Table 7 reports mean F1 0.564 for SMAP and 0.622 for MSL, while Table 2 reports CCM-TAD best F1 of 0.524 for SMAP and 0.619 for MSL. A best score cannot be lower than a mean over runs unless the tables use different protocols or contain errors, and the manuscript does not explain this.

The causality motivation is questionable for a reconstruction-based detector. At time t the window contains only past and current observations, so a non-causal mixer over the window cannot leak future information about x_t. The causal mask may act only as a regularizer, yet the paper repeatedly claims causality is necessary and that it is the first to address a fundamental limitation.

The abstract and introduction claim 'consistently' superior F1, but the model ties SensitiveHUE(Online) on SMAP and is worse than SensitiveHUE(Offline) on SWaT. The claim is overstated and should be softened or qualified.

Baseline fairness is not fully established. The authors create an 'online' SensitiveHUE by removing robust normalization, but their own model uses test-set-tuned alpha/h, and it is unclear whether baselines were given the same threshold-selection protocol. This makes the main comparison difficult to interpret.

The causal linear layer uses an upper-triangular mask with entries 1/j rather than a standard binary causal mask. No justification is provided for this particular scaling, and it may unnecessarily restrict or bias the learned temporal transformation.

Ablations are narrow: the modular ablation in Table 4 covers only SWaT and PSM, and the clustering-variant comparison in Table 5 also covers only those two datasets. The robustness of the architectural conclusions across all six benchmarks is therefore unclear.
No code release or anonymized implementation is referenced, and the inconsistent table values reduce confidence that the reported numbers are reproducible.
The backward-search labels for onset/offset are retrospective and may delay or reframe anomaly decisions, so the full proposed pipeline is not strictly online even apart from threshold tuning.

strengths: Combines three reasonable ideas (a causally-masked MLP-Mixer, correlation-based channel clustering with per-cluster embeddings, and a sequential/CUSUM-style anomaly score) into one model, with a coherent architecture and clear diagram (Figures 1).

Empirical coverage is broad: six public benchmark datasets and 15 baselines, and the authors re-run SensitiveHUE's public code to construct an 'online' variant, showing awareness that offline robust normalization is not real-time compatible.

Includes a modular ablation, a clustering-variant ablation (Table 5), a 3-seed robustness table with standard deviations, a GFLOPs cost table, and a genuinely informative limitations section (parameter reduction analysis, temporal-mixer expansion-factor caveat, α sensitivity).
Correctly avoids the discredited point-adjusted F1 metric and explains why (long anomaly segments are over-rewarded), which is good practice.
The embedding-parameter reduction argument O(C·d) → O(C·d/M) is mathematically sound and empirically plausible.
weaknesses: The reported evaluation is dominated by test-set threshold tuning: Appendix D states 'We search for the best α and h values for the anomaly detection method to get the best F1 score.' The validation set is used only to build the p-value reference distribution, while the decision threshold that determines detections is chosen on the test set. This directly contradicts the paper's central 'online/real-time' claim (which is also the stated justification for downgrading SensitiveHUE to an 'online' variant) and inflates the headline F1 numbers relative to any fixed-threshold online method.

Internal inconsistency between the main and appendix tables undermines confidence in the numbers. Table 2 reports 'best' F1 of 0.524 for SMAP and 0.619 for MSL, yet Table 7 reports 3-seed means of 0.564 (SMAP) and 0.622 (MSL) — i.e., a mean exceeds the reported 'best,' which is impossible if the tables describe the same model. No explanation is given.

The head-to-head comparison is largely apples-to-oranges: all baselines except SensitiveHUE are copied from NPSR/SensitiveHUE papers, which use different preprocessing, normalization, and evaluation protocols. Given known sensitivity of MTS anomaly detection to these choices, the reported 10–12% 'improvements' on PSM/MSL/SMD are not reliably attributable to the proposed model.

The ablation conclusions are overstated relative to noise. Runs vary by std = 0.008–0.025 (Table 7), yet claims such as 'the causal temporal mixer effectively captures the temporal information' rest on differences like SWaT Case 9 (0.875) vs Case 8 (0.871) and Case 6 (0.874), which are within a fraction of one standard deviation. No significance testing is provided.

The causality motivation is weak. For reconstruction over a look-back window that consists entirely of past data at inference time, bidirectional mixing is not a data-leakage problem, so the argument that 'systems are causal... present data is only influenced by past data points' does not fundamentally require causal mixing. The masking scheme with γ_{i,j}=1/j (Eq. 11) is ad hoc and its scaling is not justified.

The sequential scoring (Eqs. 14–17) is essentially a CUSUM/SPRT-style accumulation with backward onset/offset search, which has substantial prior art (the paper itself cites Doshi/Yilmaz). Presenting it as a novel contribution overstates originality.

Presentation problems: the Table 4 caption states '× and ✓ denote the presence and absence of each module,' which is reversed relative to the table/table text (✓ denotes the proposed clustered configuration), making the ablation hard to parse; Eq. 4's definition refers to L2 rather than L2'.

The headline claim of 'consistently superior F1' is not supported: the model loses to SensitiveHUE (Offline) on SWaT (0.883 vs 0.911) and only matches the SensitiveHUE (Online) value on SMAP (0.524), so improvements are dataset-dependent rather than consistent.

strengths: The paper targets an important and practical problem: online anomaly detection in multivariate time series, and it explicitly avoids the test-set-dependent robust normalization used by SensitiveHUE, which is relevant for real-time deployment.

The proposed architecture combines several sensible ideas: a causal MLP-Mixer variant that masks temporal linear layers to respect temporal ordering, cluster-aware multi-embedding via spectral clustering of channel correlation profiles, and a sequential anomaly-evidence accumulation scheme.

Empirical evaluation is broad: six public benchmarks, fifteen baselines, no point adjustment, and an online reimplementation of SensitiveHUE for fair comparison. The model improves F1 on WADI, PSM, MSL, and SMD and matches the best online result on SMAP.

Ablations isolate the contributions of channel clustering, causal temporal mixing, embedding mixing, and sequential anomaly scoring. The spurious-correlation experiment in Appendix G provides direct evidence that cluster-aware embeddings reduce cross-channel spurious correlations.
The paper is generally reproducible: it reports preprocessing, hyperparameter search ranges, hardware, random seeds, and GFLOPs, and it includes an honest limitations section.
The online sequential detection method improves recall over point-based MSE thresholding in Table 3, supporting the claim that evidence accumulation reduces missed detections.
weaknesses: The evaluation protocol uses test labels to tune the anomaly-detection hyperparameters α and h: Appendix D states “We search for the best α and h values ... to get the best F1 score.” This is test-set leakage and undermines the paper’s central online claim. The reported F1 scores may be optimistic; thresholds should be selected on validation data or fixed, and AUROC/AP should be reported.

The causality claim is not fully established. The paper applies 1D batch normalization to representations of shape L×d and inside the mixer; if normalization is performed over the temporal dimension, future information can leak across time steps. The paper does not specify the normalization axes clearly, so the strict causal guarantee is questionable.

The causal temporal mixer is essentially a masked linear layer with expansion factor 1. The claim that an expansion factor greater than 1 cannot maintain causality is not justified, since a hidden expansion with separate causal masks would still be causal. This limits the architectural contribution.

Ablation coverage is limited. The modular ablation in Table 4 only covers SWaT and PSM; Table 5 only PSM and SWaT; Table 3 omits SMAP. Main results in Table 2 are best F1 without variance or significance tests, so the robustness of the reported improvements is not fully demonstrated.

Baseline comparisons rely mostly on numbers reported in prior papers with potentially different preprocessing/evaluation protocols. Only SensitiveHUE is rerun. D3R results are missing for PSM and SMAP, and SensitiveHUE (Offline) still substantially outperforms the proposed model on SWaT, so the “consistently superior” claim is overstated.

The novelty is incremental. Masked causal linear layers are a straightforward adaptation, and spectral clustering of correlation profiles is standard. The paper does not disentangle how much of the gain comes from the architecture versus the sequential scoring and test-set threshold tuning.

Reproducibility is incomplete: no code link is provided, exact per-dataset hyperparameters (e.g., M, d, d_f, learning rate) are not fully reported, and some notation is ambiguous (e.g., the Table 4 caption contradicts the main text about ×/✓).
Practical online efficiency is not demonstrated. The paper reports GFLOPs but no latency or runtime comparison against baselines, and WADI requires 17.1 GFLOPs, which may limit real-time use.

strengths: The paper provides a comprehensive empirical evaluation on six public benchmark datasets against 23 baselines, including multiple evaluation protocols for multi-entity datasets and additional metrics (PR_AUC, VUS_PR, VUS_ROC) in the appendix.

The sequential anomaly scoring method is well-motivated and statistically interpreted (Appendix A), and the ablation in Table 4 shows it improves over point-based detection across most datasets (e.g., PSM 0.657→0.716, MSL 0.557→0.638).

The cluster-aware multi-embedding is a reasonable approach to reducing spurious inter-channel correlations; Table 14 and Figure 9 provide direct evidence of reduced spurious correlation, and Table 5 shows clustering improves performance in the full model.

The model is relatively lightweight: Table 13 reports fewer GFLOPs than SensitiveHUE (Online) on all datasets and fewer parameters on SWAT, PSM, WADI, and SMAP, with inference times on the order of milliseconds per batch, supporting practical deployment.

The paper includes a range of ablations, sensitivity analyses, robustness across random seeds (Table 12), and an explicit limitations section, demonstrating thorough experimentation and awareness of scope.
weaknesses: The central motivation for the causal mixer is questionable. In the described online reconstruction setting, the model inputs X_L = {x_{t-L+1},...,x_t} and reconstructs only the latest observation x_t. Since all inputs are past/current, a non-causal temporal mixer over the window does not use future information beyond time t. The causal mask only prevents earlier positions within the window from seeing later positions, but those later positions are still available at inference time. The gradient analysis (Figure 3) evaluates the reconstruction loss at an intermediate time t=15 with future indices τ>15, which is inconsistent with the method's stated training/inference objective of reconstructing only the latest observation. This undermines the first and most emphasized contribution.

The online detection claim is not fully supported by the primary evaluation. The best-F1 metric is obtained by sweeping α and h over the test set using ground-truth labels (Eq. 24), which is impossible in a real online deployment. The paper does not report performance with a threshold selected solely from validation data, so the practical online detection performance remains unclear.

Some claims are overstated. The abstract and conclusion state that the method 'consistently achieves superior performance,' but SensitiveHUE (Offline) achieves 0.911 best-F1 on SWAT versus CCM-TAD's 0.883, and on PSM PR_AUC CCM-TAD (0.558) is lower than xLSTMAD (0.598). The paper acknowledges these exceptions but does not sufficiently temper its general claims.

Technical and presentation inconsistencies hinder reproducibility and readability. Eq. (11) defines γ_{i,j}=1/i but the text and Appendix J.4 describe 1/j scaling; the NN-sep definition in Section 4.2.3 has identical numerator and denominator; Table 5 caption reverses the ×/✓ semantics; and many reference years are incorrect (e.g., Entekhabi et al., 2024 vs. 2010; Faber et al., 2020 vs. 2025; Saito et al., 2018 vs. 2015).

The clustering benefits are modest and not always aligned with the claimed mechanism. Ablation gains from clustering are small (e.g., SWAT 0.865→0.883, PSM 0.703→0.716), and Table 6 shows only a 0.06% NN-sep improvement on PSM despite a notable F1 improvement, weakening the separability argument.

Main comparisons lack statistical significance testing. Only a subset of results (Table 12) reports mean and standard deviation over five seeds; the primary tables report single numbers, making it difficult to judge whether improvements over baselines are statistically meaningful.

Hyperparameter tuning details are incomplete. It is unclear whether Optuna tunes the number of clusters M, embedding dimension d, α, and other hyperparameters on validation or test data. If tuning uses test performance, reported results are optimistic. The α search range is extremely broad for some datasets (e.g., [0,1) for MSL, SMAP, SMD), raising concerns about overfitting.

Reproducibility is limited by missing details. The code URL is absent from the PDF, and the manuscript does not clarify whether all points in the look-back window are reconstructed during training or only the final point, despite this being critical for interpreting the causal-mixer experiments.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and well-motivated gap: existing MLP-Mixer time-series models lack temporal causality (unlike masked transformers), and the proposed masked causal linear layer is a principled, simple fix. The gradient-based analysis (Fig. 3) convincingly shows that gradients for future time steps are suppressed in the causal variant, directly supporting the causality claim.

Cluster-aware multi-embedding driven by spectral clustering on channel correlation profiles is a plausible mechanism for mitigating spurious inter-channel correlations, and it is supported by reasonably designed ablations (Table 5 modular study, Table 7 clustering variants) and a quantitative separability analysis (NN-sep, Table 6).

The sequential anomaly-scoring method is well-motivated, has a statistical interpretation (Appendix A), and is genuinely online in the sense that it uses no test-set statistics, giving a real practical advantage over SensitiveHUE (Offline), which normalizes using the entire test set.

The empirical study is broad: six benchmark datasets, 23 baselines, three multi-entity evaluation protocols, several metrics (best-F1, PR_AUC, VUS_PR/ROC, R_F1/Aff_F1), seed-based robustness (Table 12), computational cost (Table 13), and extensive hyperparameter/appendix detail.

The appendix provides concrete reproducibility enablers (data preprocessing steps, hyperparameter search ranges, hardware, clustering pseudocode), and the ADD-FAP trade-off (Fig. 8) is a relevant evaluation for online detection.
weaknesses: Overstated central claim. The abstract/introduction assert the method 'consistently achieves superior performance,' but CCM-TAD (0.883) is clearly beaten by SensitiveHUE (Offline) (0.911) on SWAT, and it consistently loses on VUS_ROC (SWAT 0.758 vs 0.828; PSM 0.545 vs 0.676; WADI 0.822 vs 0.857). VUS_ROC is dismissed as 'less informative' without justification beyond generic imbalance arguments, and the reported '+8.71%/+8.65%' gains for WADI/PSM appear computed against offline baselines even though the text argues the online variant is the appropriate comparison point. This selective framing does not support the stated claim.

Evaluation methodology is questionable and likely inflates results. Best-F1 is obtained by sweeping thresholds on the test set, and the proposed scoring adds several additional test-tunable hyperparameters (alpha, h, delta) plus boundary refinement. Table 4 shows the scoring/boundary machinery—not the proposed architecture—accounts for the bulk of the headline improvement on PSM (0.659 -> 0.716) and large shares on MSL/SMD, so the architecture's contribution is overstated relative to a post-hoc scoring scheme designed to maximize test F1.

Pervasive presentation errors that impede understanding and trust: the Table 5 caption reverses the checkmark/cross semantics and contradicts the statement that Case 10 is the complete configuration; the causal mask is written as 1/i in Eq. (11) but described as 1/j in the text; the NN-sep definition writes E[d(a->n)]/E[d(a->n)] (denominator should be d(n->n)); there are numerous typos and malformed superscripts (e.g., '10-5', stray baseline row labels).

Reproducibility is compromised: the advertised code link is blank ('Code is available at:'), and many baseline numbers are transcribed from NPSR rather than reproduced, raising the risk of preprocessing/protocol mismatches that could favor the proposed method.

Limited originality. The 'causal linear layer' is essentially a masked linear layer analogous to causal attention masking, and spectral clustering plus CUSUM-style evidence accumulation are established techniques; the contribution is a coherent but incremental combination rather than a new understanding or mechanism.

Insufficient statistical rigor for the largest gains: variance is reported only for SWAT/PSM/WADI (Table 12), while the biggest claimed improvements (e.g., MSL protocol-3: +41.2%) are given without error bars or significance testing, and the multi-entity protocol-1 results (MSL 0.370, SMD 0.300, SMAP 0.389) are weak in absolute terms, making cross-protocol comparisons hard to interpret.

strengths: The paper proposes a coherent online anomaly detection framework that combines a causal MLP-Mixer, cluster-aware multi-embedding, and a sequential anomaly-scoring method with boundary refinement. The components are well integrated and address practical limitations of prior reconstruction-based methods.

Empirical evaluation is extensive: six public benchmark datasets, 23 baselines, and multiple metrics including best-F1, PR_AUC, VUS_PR/ROC, robustness across seeds, and computational cost. The proposed method achieves strong improvements on several datasets, especially WADI, PSM, and multi-entity datasets under multiple evaluation protocols.

Ablation studies show the contributions of channel clustering, causal temporal mixing, embedding mixing, and sequential scoring with boundary correction. The gradient-based analysis provides direct evidence that the causal mixer suppresses future information flow within the temporal mixing operation.

Online applicability is convincingly argued: the scoring method uses only past observations and validation-set statistics, avoids test-time normalization that requires future data, and has low inference latency. The paper contrasts this with SensitiveHUE's offline normalization.
The limitations section is honest and clearly scopes the work to temporal causality and multivariate settings. The impact statement is appropriately cautious.

Reproducibility is partially supported through detailed hyperparameter search ranges, hardware specifications, preprocessing steps, baseline sources, and robustness results. The method is simple enough to be reimplemented.
weaknesses: The motivation for the causal mixer is overstated. Since the model reconstructs only the latest observation in the look-back window, all inputs in that window are already past relative to the detection time t. A non-causal mixer's last output also cannot use future information beyond t. The gradient analysis evaluates a position t=15 inside a window that contains future points 16-24, which is not the actual online detection setting. The causal mask may act as a regularizer rather than preventing future leakage at detection time. Appendix K acknowledges this, but the main text claims future leakage is eliminated.

There is an inconsistency in the causal mask normalization: Eq. (11) defines gamma_{i,j}=1/i for i<=j, while the text and Appendix J.4 refer to 1/j scaling. This is a technical error that affects reproducibility and the stated optimization rationale.

The evaluation relies on best-F1 with threshold sweeping on the test set, which is an oracle-style protocol common in time-series anomaly detection but can overstate practical performance. Main tables report single runs without confidence intervals, and some improvements are small (e.g., SWAT 0.883 vs 0.874 online SensitiveHUE). Claims of 'consistently' outperforming baselines are overstated: SensitiveHUE (Offline) is better on SWAT, CCM-TAD is not best in PSM PR_AUC, and VUS_ROC is often worse.

The multi-entity protocol-3 comparison is limited: only SensitiveHUE variants are shown under protocol 3, so the claim of outperforming 'all baselines' across each protocol is not fully supported. Table 2 is also confusing because superscripts *1/*2/*3 appear for single-entity datasets where the protocol distinction does not apply.

The modular ablation (Table 5) is only on SWAT and PSM, with single runs and no error bars. The conclusion that a non-causal temporal mixer does not capture temporal information is not strongly supported by the evidence.
It is unclear whether the model reconstructs all positions in the look-back window or only the last position during training. This ambiguity affects both the causality argument and reproducibility.

The code availability link is missing in the manuscript (Figure 1 says 'Code is available at:' with no URL). It is also unclear whether the validation set used for p-value computation is the same as the validation set used for hyperparameter tuning, which could introduce overfitting to validation data.

Several baseline results are copied from different sources and protocols, which may not be directly comparable despite the paper's attempts to control for this. The paper should more clearly separate results it reproduced from results taken from prior work.
